blocks.c: Wen's instruction was written on a fire door in block capitals and I had copied it into the log before I got in the car, which is the only reason I obeyed it, because a thing you have written out in your own hand at 03:11 is much harder to talk yourself out of at 03:19.
If the numbers ever go out of order, get out at the next door and walk.

The next door was right there. The doors were open. I was standing in the car with a book in my hand looking at a floor sign that had skipped two numbers, and every single part of me wanted to press the button again and see what happened.
I want you to understand how much I wanted to press it.

Minus six was a plant room. Our plant room, actually — B2's plant room, the one I walk four times a night, chiller, pumps, sprinkler riser, the fluorescent tube by the pump room door doing its November flicker. Identical. Complete. Except that on the equipment schedule board, where somebody in 1974 had written the asset numbers in grease pencil, all the numbers were wrong in the same direction: every one exactly one hundred lower than upstairs.
I wrote that down. I found the stair.

Every building has a stair. That is the thing about this place I have come to rely on: whatever it is, it obeys its own drawings. There is always a stair, it is always in the north-east corner, and the door always opens outward with a push bar, because that is what the code required in 1974.
I went down the stair. Minus seven. Minus eight.
I could hear something from below and it took me a whole flight to work out what it was, because it was so ordinary that my brain filed it as background before it filed it as impossible.
Somewhere below me, on minus nine, at 03:40 in the morning, under a building with no floors, something was making copies.
